Scaling limit of a queue

Words: 330 Articles: 5
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
An asymptotic description obtained by increasing queue resources or input size, or by approaching critical load while rescaling time and workload. Large-buffer queue scaling, many-source queue scaling, moderate-deviation queue scaling and the heavy-traffic limit of a queue preserve different relations between mean load, random fluctuations and storage.

Heavy-traffic limit of a queue (εQε​(⌊t/ε2⌋)⇒Γ(σB(t)−dt))

Words: 63
Scaling limit of a queue OurBigBook.com
For fixed independent and identically distributed arrivals of mean μ and positive finite variance σ2, put service at μ+εd. Rescaling net input by space ε and time ε−2 gives Brownian motion with drift −d by the functional central limit theorem. The continuous Skorokhod reflection map on the half-line gives the displayed transient limit, with a correspondingly scaled initial workload. A stationary approximation additionally requires justification of limit interchange. When valid, the stationary law of negatively drifted reflected Brownian motion predicts P(Qε​>b/ε)≈e−2db/σ2.

Moderate-deviation queue scaling (logP(overflow)∼−C2Lβ/(2λ))

Words: 49
Scaling limit of a queue OurBigBook.com
For a bufferless queue with Poisson mean input Lλ, place the service margin at CL(1+β)/2, 0<β<1. It exceeds the ordinary square-root fluctuation scale but is sublinear in total input. The Poisson moderate deviation principle gives the displayed overflow exponent. This interpolates between a central-limit safety margin and a fixed per-source excess capacity.

Many-source queue scaling (L−1logP(QL​>Lb)→−infn≥1​In​(b+cn))

Words: 69
Scaling limit of a queue OurBigBook.com
Scale independent source count, service and buffer by the same factor L. For lookback horizon n, the source-average cumulative input has rate function In​, and reaching buffer level b requires input above b+cn. Optimizing this horizon gives the displayed exponent under uniform control of the infinite stationary supremum. For independent slots, In​(x)=nIA​(x/n); discrete time keeps n an integer. Temporal dependence instead enters through the cumulative-input cumulant-generating function.

Large-buffer queue scaling (b−1logP(Q>b)→−θ∗​)

Words: 114 Articles: 1
Scaling limit of a queue OurBigBook.com
Hold a stable input law and service rate of a queue fixed while the buffer size of a queue grows. Under interior exponential-moment and root hypotheses, the Cramér-Lundberg workload exponent gives an exponential tail linear in buffer size. A likely overflow accumulates during a lookback horizon proportional to the buffer size.

Cramér-Lundberg workload exponent (ΛA​(θ∗​)=cθ∗​,θ∗​=inft>0​tIA​(c+1/t))

Words: 76
Large-buffer queue scaling OurBigBook.com
For nondegenerate independent and identically distributed arrivals with mean below c, suppose the positive root is interior to the moment-generating function domain. Then ΛA′​(θ∗​)>c. The Fenchel–Young inequality gives tIA​(c+1/t)≥θ∗​ for every t>0, and equality occurs at t=[ΛA′​(θ∗​)−c]−1. The exponential workload bound from cumulative arrival moments gives the upper logarithmic tail bound for every θ<θ∗​. A horizon of the indicated length times buffer size gives the matching lower bound by Cramér's theorem. A positive interior root is an assumption; if arrivals never exceed capacity, positive workload cannot arise.

Geometric-arrival single-service queue (Xn+1​=max(Xn​−1,0)+Gn​)

Words: 76
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
Let the independent arrivals satisfy Pr(Gn​=j)=qpj, with p+q=1. During a busy period, each served customer produces Gn​ further customers, so the total number served has the total-progeny law of a Galton-Watson process with mean p/q. Its extinction probability solves s=q/(1−ps) and is the smaller of 1 and q/p. The queue is positive recurrent for p<1/2, null recurrent for p=1/2, and transient for p>1/2. In the positive recurrent case its stationary distribution is πj​=(1−p/q)(p/q)j.

General-service infinite-server queue (M/G/∞)

Words: 143 Articles: 1
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
Poisson arrivals of rate λ receive independent service times distributed as S, with infinitely many servers so service starts on arrival. Starting empty, the occupancy at time t is Poisson with mean λ∫0t​P(S>u)du, by independent thinning of the marked arrivals. If ES<∞, the equilibrium count is Poisson with mean λES. Occupancy need not be a Markov process for a general service law; remaining service times carry additional state information.

Clearance time after closing an infinite-server queue (P(VE>v)=1−e−λE(S−v)+​)

Words: 67
General-service infinite-server queue OurBigBook.com
Stop new arrivals at time t in an initially empty general-service infinite-server queue. The number remaining v time units later is Poisson with mean λ∫vt+v​P(S>u)du. Thus the probability that clearance has not occurred is one minus the exponential of the negative of that mean. Letting t→∞ gives the displayed equilibrium formula, since ∫v∞​P(S>u)du=E(S−v)+​. The clearance time is zero when no customers remain at closing.

Alternating arrival and service queue (θ=λ(μ+β)/[μ(λ+α)])

Words: 75
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
A continuous-time Markov chain may alternate between an arrival phase C, with upward transitions at rate λ, and a service phase W, with downward transitions at rate μ when the level is positive. Switching rates C→W and W→C are α,β. Its stationary balance equations give a geometric invariant tail with ratio θ=λ(μ+β)/[μ(λ+α)]. A stationary probability exists exactly when μα>λβ, consistent with the stationary average service rate μα/(α+β) exceeding the arrival rate λβ/(α+β).

Queue (queueing theory)

Words: 1k Articles: 19
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
A queue consists of customers or jobs waiting for or receiving service. An arrival process adds customers and a service rule specifies which waiting customer is served next. A stochastic model of these events is studied in queueing theory; its queue length is the number of customers waiting or in service, according to the stated convention.

Burstiness of queue input

Words: 42
Queue (queueing theory) OurBigBook.com
The size and frequency of unusually large arrivals or sustained overload episodes. It depends on the time and threshold scales being examined, rather than just on the one-slot variance. A cap can leave smaller rare deviations unchanged while removing larger positive bursts.

Bufferless queue

Words: 233 Articles: 4
Queue (queueing theory) OurBigBook.com
A queue which retains no unfinished work between slots. Given nonnegative input A and capacity c, its bufferless queue output is min(A,c) and its lost work is (A−c)+.

Poisson large-service overflow asymptotic (logP(X>c)=−clog(c/λ)+c−λ+O(logc))

Words: 54
Bufferless queue OurBigBook.com
For fixed Poisson mean λ>0 and capacity c→∞, set m=⌊c⌋+1. The optimized Chernoff bound gives logP(X≥m)≤−IP​(m). The lower bound by P(X=m) and Stirling's formula differs by only O(logm). Rounding m to c changes the cost by O(logc), proving the displayed formula and the leading scale −clogc.

Bufferless queue output (Y=min(A,c),W=(A−c)+)

Words: 153 Articles: 2
Bufferless queue OurBigBook.com
The work served in one slot is capped at the service rate of a queue. The remainder is lost, so output is input minus its positive part above capacity. Every downstream threshold below the cap has exactly the same overflow event for input and output; thresholds at or above the cap cannot be exceeded by the output.
Moderate deviation scales of a clipped Poisson aggregate (Kβ​(y)=y2/(2λ) (y≤C),Kβ​(y)=∞ (y>C))
Words: 48
Bufferless queue output OurBigBook.com
Clip Poisson input of mean Lλ at Lλ+CL(1+β)/2. The Poisson moderate deviation principle and contraction principle for large deviations give the displayed output rate at the clipping scale. At smaller exponents the output retains the original rate by moderate deviations below a bufferless queue cap. At larger positive-deviation scales every overflow event is eventually impossible because the requested threshold exceeds the cap.
Moderate deviations below a bufferless queue cap (α<β:SL​ and min(SL​,uL​) are exponentially equivalent at speed Lα)
Words: 54
Bufferless queue output OurBigBook.com
For Poisson input and uL​=Lλ+CL(1+β)/2 with C>0, clipping occurs with logarithmic probability −C2Lβ/(2λ). At any smaller exponent 0<α<β, this is superexponentially small at speed Lα. Dividing the input and output difference by L(1+α)/2 therefore gives exponential equivalence. More directly, for every threshold rL​<uL​, the events {min(SL​,uL​)>rL​} and {SL​>rL​} are identical.

Queue overflow

Words: 47
Queue (queueing theory) OurBigBook.com
An arrival exceeds the available service and storage capacity, causing work to be lost or blocked. For a bufferless queue with capacity c per slot, overflow means input work strictly greater than c. Stationary queue workload tails in an infinite-buffer comparison model are often used to estimate finite-buffer overflow probabilities.

Buffer size of a queue (b)

Words: 26
Queue (queueing theory) OurBigBook.com
The maximum stored work or number of waiting jobs, according to the model's convention. A bufferless queue has no room to retain excess input for a later slot.

Service rate of a queue (c)

Words: 24
Queue (queueing theory) OurBigBook.com
The amount of work a queue can serve per unit of time. In a slotted model the same units can describe work served per slot.

Queueing delay (Wq​)

Words: 58
Queue (queueing theory) OurBigBook.com
The queueing delay is the time between a customer's arrival and the start of its service, excluding its own service time. Under first come first served with service rate C, its queueing delay is the queue workload ahead of it divided by C. The customer sojourn time also includes the customer's own service. In a preemptive priority queue with a shared buffer, a voice customer's initial waiting time depends only on the voice queue workload already present.

Workload of a queue (W)

Words: 681 Articles: 8
Queue (queueing theory) OurBigBook.com
The queue workload of a queue is the total remaining service work of all present customers, including residual work in service. With a work-conserving server of rate C and stationary input A, the stationary queue workload is represented by
W(0)=supt≥0​{A(−t,0]−Ct}.
(1)
This is the amount by which past offered work exceeds available service, maximized over possible starts of a busy period. It is the reflection of net input at zero. Under first come first served, an arriving infinitesimal customer waits W/C; a priority customer instead waits for the remaining work ahead of it under its service discipline.

Stationary workload supremum (Q=dsupn≥0​(∑j=1n​Aj​−cn))

Words: 51
Workload of a queue OurBigBook.com
For independent and identically distributed arrivals with finite mean below service c, the strong law of large numbers makes the net cumulative input tend to minus infinity, so the supremum is finite almost surely. Applying the same formula to the past input gives a stationary solution of the Lindley recursion. This representation turns queue workload overflow into an event involving some lookback horizon.

Linear workload rate for a local convex action (J(x)=xinfv>C​g(v)/(v−C),x>0)

Words: 75
Workload of a queue OurBigBook.com
For a stable input with path action I(a)=∫−∞0​g(a˙s​)ds, a workload x requires some interval of length t with average input near C+x/t. Jensen inequality bounds its cost below by tg(C+x/t); taking the supremum workload and then the infimum over t yields the displayed lower bound. Constant-rate burst paths give the matching upper bound. At zero the typical-rate path has zero cost; negative workloads have infinite rate. If no finite-cost rate exceeds C, every positive workload has infinite rate.

Constant-rate burst path (t=x/(v−C),v>C)

Words: 89
Workload of a queue OurBigBook.com
Use arrival rate v during the last t time units and the normal stable rate mu before that, where μ<C. The lookback net input increases from zero to x over the burst, then decreases because the earlier net drift is negative. Its infinite-buffer workload is x, as is the finite-buffer workload map for capacity at least x. For a local convex path cost with density g and g(μ)=0, its cost is tg(v)=xg(v)/(v−C). These paths realize or approximate the optimal workload cost even if an optimizing duration is not attained.

Finite-buffer workload map (0≤qˉ​B​(a)≤min(q(a),B))

Words: 218 Articles: 2
Workload of a queue OurBigBook.com
With lookback net input z(s)=a(−s,0]−Cs, the stable finite-buffer workload is supt≥0​min(sup0≤s≤t​z(s),B+inf0≤s≤t​z(s)). Since z(0)=0, it lies between zero and B, and is at most the infinite-buffer supremum q(a)=sups≥0​z(s). For a constant-rate burst which builds exactly x work from an empty queue, no upper reflection occurs when x≤B and both workloads equal x.
Finite-memory continuity of a finite-buffer queue (∣QB​(x)−QB​(y)∣≤T2∥x−y∥)
Words: 94
Finite-buffer workload map OurBigBook.com
Use the clipped Lindley recursion qt+1​=min(B,max(0,qt​+xt​−C)) and the weighted cumulative-input topology for a slotted queue. If cumulative past input Sx​(T)≤λT eventually with λ<C, choose a finite T so Sx​(T)−CT<−B. Starting with a full buffer at time −T, the queue must hit zero before the present, since otherwise its final workload is at most B+Sx​(T)−CT<0. Monotonicity couples all initial workloads by that zero, establishing a finite memory horizon. The same horizon works for sufficiently close input y. Since ∣x−k​−y−k​∣≤(2k−1)∥x−y∥ and clipping is Lipschitz continuous with constant one, the two finite recursions started empty differ by at most ∑k=1T​(2k−1)∥x−y∥=T2∥x−y∥.
Finite-buffer workload rate truncation (JˉB​(x)=J(x) (0≤x≤B),JˉB​(x)=∞ otherwise)
Words: 65
Finite-buffer workload map OurBigBook.com
For the local convex action defining the linear workload rate for a local convex action, continuity and the contraction principle for large deviations give workload rate functions. The pointwise bound qˉ​B​≤q makes JˉB​(x)≥infy≥x​J(y)=J(x) on nonnegative workloads. Constant-rate burst paths produce the reverse bound for x at most B. Values outside the buffer interval are impossible. This statement concerns the rate at the workload value, rather than equality of exact finite-buffer and infinite-buffer stationary distributions.

Lindley recursion (Wk+1​=(Wk​+Zk+1​)+)

Words: 159 Articles: 1
Workload of a queue OurBigBook.com
For arrivals added before the slot's offered service, Zk​ is the arriving work minus that service. With independent identically distributed increments of negative mean, the stationary queue workload has the law supm≥0​∑j=1m​Zj​. Iterating the recursion from the past gives this supremum; the strong law makes it finite. A different arrival/service ordering changes slot-boundary workload but requires its convention to be stated.
Slower-server tandem workload identity (R(a,c,d)=Q(a,d)−Q(a,c),d<c)
Words: 99
Lindley recursion OurBigBook.com
Consider two work-conserving slotted queues in tandem, with upstream service c and downstream service d<c, where upstream departures can be served downstream in the same slot. Put Dt​=min{c,Qt−1​+at​}. Then Qt​=Qt−1​+at​−Dt​ and Rt​=(Rt−1​+Dt​−d)+. If Rt−1​+Dt​≥d, addition gives (Qt−1​+Rt−1​+at​−d)+. Otherwise Dt​<d<c, so the upstream queue empties and both sides of that identity are zero. Thus total workload obeys the Lindley recursion with service d. Starting empty in the remote past yields the displayed identity whenever the upstream workload is finite. Both workloads, and hence their difference, are continuous in the weighted cumulative-input topology for a slotted queue under strictly subcritical mean input λ<d<c.

Heterogeneous two-server queue (μ=μ1​+μ2​)

Words: 93
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
A queue with a Poisson process of arrivals and two independent service times with exponential distributions of different rates must distinguish the two possible single-customer states. If an arrival chooses either idle server with probability 1/2, the continuous-time Markov chain is reversible. Write a,b for the states with only server one or two busy, and n≥2 for total population. Its detailed balance equations give πa​=π0​ν/(2μ1​), πb​=π0​ν/(2μ2​) and πn​=π0​ν2(ν/μ)n−2/(2μ1​μ2​). These weights normalize exactly when ν<μ. In equilibrium, reversed upward transitions have total rate ν in every state, so time reversal of a continuous-time Markov chain makes the departure stream a Poisson process of rate ν. This output conclusion requires stationarity.

Busy period (B)

Words: 110 Articles: 1
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
A busy period is the interval from an arrival that finds the system empty until the next departure leaving it empty. It excludes the preceding idle waiting time. In a stable M/G/1 queue with arrival rate λ and mean service time m, its mean is m/(1−λm).

Busy-period branching equation (ϕB​(θ)=ϕS​(θ+λ(ϕB​(θ)−1)))

Words: 65
Busy period OurBigBook.com
In an M/G/1 queue, arrivals during the first service generate independent subtrees of work. Conditional on service time S=s, the number of descendants is Poisson with mean λs. Thus B=dS+∑j=1N(S)​Bj​, with independent descendant busy periods. Conditioning and the Poisson generating function give the displayed transform equation wherever its moment-generating functions are finite. Taking expectations yields EB=ES+λESEB in the stable regime.

Multiclass single-server queue

Words: 338 Articles: 2
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
An ordered state x=(c1​,…,cn​) records the classes and positions of customers at a single server. Class-r arrivals have rate αr​ and exponential service parameter μr​. Under a symmetric service discipline, its stationary distribution is (1−ρ)∏i​(αci​​/μci​​), where ρ=∑r​αr​/μr​<1. If every μr​=μ, class-independent insertion and service position rules need not be equal: time reversal of a continuous-time Markov chain interchanges them and proves the same law. Aggregating words gives (1−ρ)n!∏r​[(αr​/μr​)nr​/nr​!] by the multinomial coefficient. With class-dependent service rates, first come first served need not have this product law.

Priority queue with a shared buffer

Words: 263 Articles: 1
Multiclass single-server queue OurBigBook.com
A two-class queue has one total buffer but serves the high-priority class before the other. A preemptive-resume service discipline interrupts low-priority work immediately and later resumes it without wasting completed work. Under first come first served within the high-priority class, a new high-priority packet waits V/C when V is the high-priority workload immediately before its arrival. The total workload determines shared-buffer overflow, while V determines the high-priority waiting time. An additional admission gate rejects high-priority packets when V/C exceeds a prescribed delay limit. Finite packets require a fit test against the remaining buffer space, and nonpreemptive service adds residual low-priority service time.

Overflow onto longer paths can create feedback and multiple solutions of the Erlang fixed point approximation, even though an exact finite irreducible occupancy Markov chain has a unique stationary distribution.
Multiple Erlang fixed points under alternative routing
Words: 174 Articles: 2
Alternative routing OurBigBook.com
A symmetric triangle with direct calls and two-link overflow routes has Erlang fixed point approximation equation B=E(λ[1+2B(1−B)],C). For C=1000 and λ=950, this has at least three solutions, certified by the intermediate value theorem using signs at B=0,0.01,0.1,0.4.
Fluid scaling proof of multiple Erlang fixed points
Words: 56
Multiple Erlang fixed points under alternative routing OurBigBook.com
Let GN​(B)=E(20N[1+2B(1−B)],21N)−B. The proportional scaling limit of the Erlang loss formula makes its limits at B=1/100 and B=1/8 respectively −1/100 and 7/520. Since GN​(0)>0 and GN​(1)<0, sufficiently large N give alternating signs at these four points. The intermediate value theorem supplies three distinct zeros in the intervening intervals. These are multiple solutions of the Erlang fixed point approximation, not multiple stationary laws of an exact finite irreducible Markov chain.
Alternative-routing triangle with three Erlang fixed points (B=E(C,v[1+2B(1−B)]))
Words: 85
Multiple Erlang fixed points under alternative routing OurBigBook.com
On a three-node loss network, each pair offers direct calls of load v to its link of capacity C. If blocked, the call tries the two-link path through the remaining node. The symmetric reduced-load approximation gives a link its direct load and two overflow contributions vB(1−B), hence the displayed equation. For C=1000, v=940, its residual has alternating signs at B=0,0.01,0.10,0.25, giving at least three distinct roots. This multiplicity belongs to the Erlang fixed point approximation, not to the exact stationary law of a finite reachable Markov chain.

Erlang loss formula (E(a,C))

Words: 444 Articles: 8
Loss network OurBigBook.com
For capacity C and offered traffic a, the probability of a full single-resource loss system is E(a,C)=(aC/C!)/(∑k=0C​ak/k!). The stable recursion is E(a,0)=1, E(a,k)=aE(a,k−1)/(k+aE(a,k−1)).
Rational certificates for the Erlang loss recursion (b0​=1,bj​=abj−1​/(j+abj−1​))
Words: 50
Erlang loss formula OurBigBook.com
For rational offered load, every step of the stable recursion for the Erlang loss formula is rational. Comparing the final numerator and denominator with rational thresholds therefore certifies signs without floating-point uncertainty. Opposite certified signs of a continuous fixed-point residual imply a root by the intermediate value theorem; several alternating intervals can prove multiple Erlang fixed points under alternative routing.
Monotonicity of the Erlang blocking probability (∂a​E(a,C)=E(a,C)[C−mC​(a)]/a>0)
Words: 63
Erlang loss formula OurBigBook.com
For positive integer capacity C and offered load a>0, let mC​(a) be the carried load of an Erlang loss resource. Differentiating the upper-truncated Poisson distribution gives mC′​(a)=Var(N)/a>0. Differentiating its probability at C gives the displayed derivative of the Erlang loss formula; it is positive because mC​(a)<C. Thus blocking increases continuously from zero to one, and the carried load increases from zero to C. These properties justify the inverse blocking coordinates in the convex potential for the Erlang fixed point.
Proportional scaling limit of the Erlang loss formula (E(Nν,NC)→max{0,1−C/ν})
Words: 66
Erlang loss formula OurBigBook.com
Scale the offered load and capacity together. Reversing the denominator of the Erlang loss formula gives
E(Nν,NC)−1=∑j=0NC​∏ℓ=0j−1​NνNC−ℓ​.
(18)
For each fixed j, the summand tends to (C/ν)j. If ν>C, the dominated convergence theorem applies with the summable geometric series bound (C/ν)j. Otherwise each fixed finite partial sum has limiting value at least its number of terms, so the reciprocal diverges. Taking reciprocals proves the formula, including the critical case ν=C.
Carried load of an Erlang loss resource (mC​(a)=a[1−E(a,C)])
Words: 45
Erlang loss formula OurBigBook.com
For offered load a and capacity C≥1, the carried load equals the mean occupancy:
mC​(a)=a[1−E(a,C)].
(19)
Differentiating the truncated-Poisson equilibrium weights gives mC′​(a)=Vara​(N)/a>0 for a>0. The carried load increases from zero to C. This monotonicity supplies the strictly increasing term in the convex potential for the Erlang fixed point.
Erlang fixed point approximation
Words: 195 Articles: 3
Erlang loss formula OurBigBook.com
The Erlang fixed point approximation treats resource blocking as independent and applies the Erlang loss formula to traffic screened by other resources. Its self-consistency equations have a unique fixed point under fixed routing, but can have several under alternative routing.
Convex potential for the Erlang fixed point (F(y))
Words: 127 Articles: 1
Erlang fixed point approximation OurBigBook.com
Set yj​=−log(1−Bj​) and let eC​(a)=E(a,C). For positive integer capacities,
U(z,C)=e−zeC−1​(1−e−z),F(y)=∑r​νr​e−(ATy)r​+∑j​∫0yj​​U(z,Cj​)dz.
(20)
The function U is the carried load of an Erlang loss resource evaluated at its inverse blocking parametrization. It is continuous and strictly increasing from zero to C. Hence F is a coercive function and a strictly convex function on the nonnegative orthant. Its first-order conditions are the fixed-routing Erlang fixed point equations, including zero prices at unused links.
Cyclic substitution for the Erlang fixed point
Words: 69
Convex potential for the Erlang fixed point OurBigBook.com
Update one link blocking probability at a time using the reduced load accepted by all other links, then cycle through the links. In logarithmic acceptance coordinates this is exact coordinate descent for the convex potential for the Erlang fixed point. Potential values decrease within a compact sublevel set. Continuity of a whole-sweep update forces every limit point to minimize every coordinate, hence to equal the unique global minimizer. This proves convergence without requiring a simultaneous substitution scheme.
Reduced-load approximation
Words: 35
Erlang fixed point approximation OurBigBook.com
For unit resource requirements in a loss network, the effective offered traffic to resource j is aj​=∑r:j∈r​αr​∏k∈r∖{j}​(1−Bk​), where Bk​ are approximate resource blocking probabilities. The resource being modeled is excluded from its own screening product.

Offered traffic (αr​=νr​/μr​)

Words: 35
Loss network OurBigBook.com
For calls arriving at rate νr​ with mean holding time 1/μr​, offered traffic is the dimensionless load αr​=νr​/μr​, often measured in Erlangs. The Erlang loss formula distinguishes this offered traffic from the mean traffic actually carried.

Fixed routing

Words: 276 Articles: 5
Loss network OurBigBook.com
Under fixed routing, each call type always requests the same collection of resources. The link-route incidence matrix records those requirements. This differs from alternative routing, in which a rejected direct request can try another route.
Product-form stationary distribution of a loss network (π(n)∝∏r​αrnr​​/nr​!)
Words: 245 Articles: 4
Fixed routing OurBigBook.com
For a loss network with feasible occupancies An≤C, its stationary distribution is proportional to ∏r​αrnr​​/nr​!. It is the law of independent Poisson random variables conditioned on the resource constraints. With exponential holding times, detailed balance for a continuous-time Markov chain proves the formula directly.
Blocking partition ratio for a loss network (Br​=1−Z(C−Ar​)/Z(C))
Words: 46
Product-form stationary distribution of a loss network OurBigBook.com
Let Z(C) sum the unnormalized occupancy weights ∏r​ρrnr​​/nr​! over feasible counts. The states admitting another type-r call are exactly those feasible under capacities C−Ar​. Poisson arrivals see time averages therefore gives the displayed blocking probability. Take Z to be zero when the reduced capacities make its feasible set empty.
Entropy maximization for loss-network occupancy (Hν​(x)=∑r​[xr​logνr​+xr​−xr​logxr​])
Words: 132 Articles: 1
Product-form stationary distribution of a loss network OurBigBook.com
For positive arrival rates and capacities with every route nonempty, maximizing Hν​(x) over x≥0, Ax≤C has a unique positive optimizer x∗. The Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions give xr∗​=νr​e−(ATz)r​ for nonnegative link prices with complementary slackness. Under proportional scaling by N, the Stirling formula gives a uniform logarithmic weight approximation logwN​(n)=NHν​(n/N)+O(logN). Strict concavity and compactness give an objective gap away from x∗, while only polynomially many feasible states exist. Thus the stationary distribution has n/N→x∗ in probability, with exponentially small probabilities outside any fixed neighborhood of x∗. In particular E[n]=Nx∗+o(N).
Poisson exponential tilting for a loss network (πN​(n)∝1{An≤NC}​ezT(An−NC)∏r​Pr{Poisson(Nxr∗​)=nr​})
Words: 40
Entropy maximization for loss-network occupancy OurBigBook.com
Substituting the optimizer relation νr​=xr∗​e(ATz)r​ into the product-form stationary distribution of a loss network proves the displayed exact identity. The independent Poisson random variables give a reference law centered at the optimized occupancies, while the constraint and exponential factor account for saturated resources. An unconstrained Gaussian approximation can miss these boundary effects.
Insensitivity of loss networks
Words: 34
Product-form stationary distribution of a loss network OurBigBook.com
For the standard fixed routing loss network with independent Poisson processes, the stationary occupancy law depends on independent holding-time distributions only through their means. The occupancy process alone need not be a Markov process when those holding times lack the memoryless property.

Poisson arrivals see time averages

Words: 39
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
The Poisson arrivals see time averages property says that an external Poisson process independent of a stationary system sees the system-state distribution at its arrival times. Thus the fraction of arrivals that accept a state-dependent admission rule p(n) is ∑n​πn​p(n).

M/G/1 queue

Words: 218 Articles: 4
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
An M/G/1 queue has Poisson arrivals, independent identically distributed service times, and one server. If service has mean m and λm<1, its mean busy period is
1−λmm​.
(21)
This follows by decomposing the busy period into the first service and the busy-period descendants of arrivals during that service.

M/D/1 queue (M/D/1)

Words: 47
M/G/1 queue OurBigBook.com
An M/D/1 queue has a Poisson process of arrivals, a deterministic service time τ, and one work-conserving server. With arrival rate λ and λτ<1, its equilibrium idle probability is 1−λτ: the stationary completed work per unit time is λτ. Its output generally need not be a Poisson process.

Embedded departure chain of an M-G-1 queue

Words: 121 Articles: 2
M/G/1 queue OurBigBook.com
Let Qn​ be the number left immediately after departure n, and let An​ be the arrivals during the next service. Then
Qn+1​=Qn​−1{Qn​>0}​+An​.
(22)
Conditional on service duration S, An​ is Poisson with parameter λS, so
EAn​=λES,EAn2​=λES+λ2ES2.
(23)

Pollaczek-Khinchine formula

Words: 75 Articles: 1
Embedded departure chain of an M-G-1 queue OurBigBook.com
For a stable first-come first-served M/G/1 queue, write ρ=λES<1 and S(s)=Ee−sS. The stationary waiting-time Laplace transform is
Wq​(s)=s−λ+λS(s)(1−ρ)s​.
(24)
With finite second service moment, differentiating at zero gives the Pollaczek-Khinchine mean formula. These are the transform and mean forms of the same queueing identity.
Pollaczek-Khinchine mean formula
Words: 30
Pollaczek-Khinchine formula OurBigBook.com
For a stable M/G/1 queue with traffic intensity ρ=λES<1, the mean waiting time before service is
Wq​=2(1−ρ)λES2​.
(25)
Equivalently, the mean number in the system is
L=ρ+2(1−ρ)λ2ES2​.
(26)

Little's law

Words: 40
Queueing theory OurBigBook.com
In a stable regenerative queue,
L=λW,
(27)
where L is mean population, λ is throughput, and W is mean sojourn time. Renewal reward proves it by identifying the area under the population path with the sum of customer sojourn times.
